newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk farmers warn govt on subsidies, wheat deficit.
newsitem.headline: Turk farmers warn govt on subsidies, wheat deficit.

text.p: Turkish farmer organisations have warned the government against policies which they say will undermine the agriculture sector and cause shortages of key staples like wheat unless strong and rapid measures are taken.

They said in separate reports that farm policies practised by the present government and its predecessors have led to uncertainties in decisions by Turkish farmers, which make up about half of Turkey's population of 65 million.

"Present practices are doomed to make Turkey a net importer of key commodities it produces, especially in wheat and other staple items," said the independent Turkish Agricultural Association (TZD) in its report.

The government's subsidy scheme, carried out in terms of support and base prices for key commodities usually announced ahead of harvest season, are the chief determining factor for farmers to choose the product to grow for that year.
"Sudsidy policies, the products to be included in the subsidy scheme and the degree of subsidies are determined arbitrarily by governments," TZD said.

The government subsidises purchases of wheat, barley, rye, corn, oats, tobacco, sugar beet, poppy, hazelnut and paddy by announcing prices usually higher than those on world markets. It also refunds farmers half of their fertiliser purchases.

But frequently changing governments and agriculture ministers have used the scheme to win votes of farmers in their own electorate who grow particular agricultural products.This coupled with probable delays in payments to producers discourages farmers in other areas from growing less-subsidised crops and causes fluctuations in national output.
Such government failure to satisfy farmers has led Turkey in the past two years to become a net importer of two key commodities -- wheat and sugar, of which it had been a net exporter previously.
"If the current conditions are continued in the production and marketing of wheat, Turkey will be forced to be a net wheat importer in the years to come," TZD said.
"With the current population growth and unless the present farm policies are abandoned, Turkey's wheat deficit is estimated to be 14 million tonnes in 2010," it said.

Turkey produces 16-17 million tonnes of wheat almost every year. It imported 1.97 million tonnes of wheat in calendar 1996, up 21.6 percent from 1995. It also imported 350,000 tonnes of sugar in 1995/96.

The government pledged to spend 107.5 trillion lira for its subsidised purchases in 1996, up from 38.6 trillion lira in 1995. It has plans to support animal husbandry and feed industry by 40 trillion lira in 1997.
The government's payments are an additionl strain on the cash-strapped treasury, which either taps international markets for loans or borrows from local banks on high rates.
Sugar beet and grain producers have asked the government for rises of 100 to 150 percent in purchase prices for 1997/98, compared to the annual inflation running around 80 percent.

The Turkish Union of Agricultural Chambers (TZOB), an influential farm organisation, said the support price policy should be modified to include more farm products and to strengthen the financial structure of purchasing agents.
"Farm Cooperatives, which act as moderators in the local market, should be enabled to buy more products from farmers otherwise farmers have trouble in selling their products," it said in its report.
"The current narrower subsidy scheme is also adding to farmers' problems," it said.
The cooperatives, which depend on sales of products they buy from farmers for money, usually resort to the treasury for help in paying for purchases.
TZOB also urged the government to bring all agriculture products under the umbrella of the Agriculture Ministry, which presently controls only grain and pulses.
--Ankara Newsroom, 90-312-446 2940
